cues.text: Let us begin with a question about regression suites that have grown unwieldy.
A regression suite grows over multiple releases.
Execution times rise, maintenance becomes expensive, and scripts are obsolete.
What should management prioritise?
Option A: delete all existing automated regression test scripts.
Option B: substitute automated execution with detailed screen logs.
Option C: discontinue all regression validation for future releases.
Option D: optimise the test portfolio through rigorous maintenance.
The provisional reviewed answer is D.
The reasoning supplied is to retain useful coverage and eliminate redundant or brittle tests.
Notice what the three wrong options have in common.
Each one throws away the protection that regression testing gives you: deleting every script, replacing execution with screen logs, or stopping regression validation altogether.
Option D keeps what is useful and removes what is redundant or brittle.
That is the right response to a suite that has become slow and costly.
Now to question fourteen.
A self-healing automation framework updates tests when interfaces change.
What evidence should prove that business-critical coverage remains intact?
Option A: systematic removal of all legacy test execution metadata.
Option B: detailed change logs and coverage impact assessments.
Option C: significant reduction in the number of automated cases.
Option D: increased complexity in user interface design visual elements.
The provisional reviewed answer is B.
The reasoning is that changes should be traceable and assessed against coverage of business-critical requirements.
When a framework changes tests automatically, you need a record of what changed, and you need an assessment of whether the coverage of business-critical requirements still holds.

Removing execution metadata would destroy evidence, cutting the number of cases says nothing about whether critical coverage survives, and making the user interface more complex has no bearing on proving coverage.
Next, question twenty-three.
A software company repeatedly fixes critical defects only to see them return in later releases.
Why is root cause analysis important?
Option A: quickly fix each defect without investigation to save development time.
Option B: ignore recurring defects, as they are unavoidable in complex environments.
Option C: rely solely on increased manual testing to catch all software issues.
Option D: identify underlying causes rather than symptoms to prevent recurrence.
The provisional reviewed answer is D.
The reasoning is that root causes must be removed to stop the same class of defect recurring.
The key distinction is between a symptom and a cause.
If you only patch the visible failure, the underlying cause is still there and the same class of defect can return in a later release.
Options A, B and C all avoid investigating why the defects happen: fixing without investigation, accepting recurrence as unavoidable, or relying only on manual testing to catch everything.
Now question twenty-four.
A secure document platform permits uploads from 1 MB to 10 MB.
Incidents occur near limits, so testers select values below, at, within, and above those thresholds.
Why?
Option A: boundary-value analysis combined with equivalence partitioning.
Option B: static review and exploratory analysis of docs.
Option C: state-transition and complex workflow testing.
Option D: compatibility and usability testing of the system.
The provisional reviewed answer is A.
The reasoning is to partition invalid and valid ranges and probe their edges to catch boundary errors.
Here the valid range is 1 MB to 10 MB.
Equivalence partitioning divides the inputs into groups that should behave alike, namely the invalid values below the range, the valid values within it, and the invalid values above it.
Boundary-value analysis then probes the edges of those groups, which is why testers choose values below, at, within, and above the 1 MB and 10 MB limits.
Since the incidents occur near the limits, that is exactly where the testing should concentrate.
Moving on to question twenty-six.
In a fully integrated e-learning environment, QA checks business requirements, security, performance and usability.
Which test level is this?
Option A: rigorous system testing in an integrated environment.
Option B: detailed code review of all application logic.
Option C: thorough integration testing of connected modules.
Option D: comprehensive component testing of isolated units.
The provisional reviewed answer is A.
The reasoning is that system testing checks end-to-end functional and quality requirements for the entire application.
The clues are the phrases fully integrated environment and the range of checks: business requirements, security, performance and usability.
Those cover the whole application, functional and quality alike.
Integration testing focuses on connected modules, component testing focuses on isolated units, and a code review is not a test level that executes the integrated system at all.
Now question thirty-one.
An AI testing tool ranks modules by historical defects but QA does not account for recent architectural changes.
What is the main risk?
Option A: previous defect patterns are irrelevant to future logic.
Option B: AI algorithms cannot process historical testing data.
Option C: new architectural risks might be ignored by the team.
Option D: design modifications do not influence testing schedules.
The provisional reviewed answer is C.
The reasoning is that past-data ranking can miss risks introduced by changed system architecture.
The tool looks backwards, ranking modules by what has failed before.
If the architecture has recently changed and QA does not factor that in, the new risks that the change introduced may be overlooked.
Notice that option A overstates the case by calling past patterns irrelevant, and options B and D make claims that the scenario does not support.
Finally, question thirty-three.
A self-healing UI test updates locators and still passes even though the workflow now submits to the wrong endpoint.
What is the key risk?
Option A: interface-based tests are inherently unreliable for complex systems.
Option B: self-healing mechanisms slow down the CI/CD execution pipeline.
Option C: automatic repairs may mask critical functional defects in software.
Option D: successful locator repair confirms the technical logic of the code.
The source lists these four options for question thirty-three but does not supply a provisional reviewed answer for it.
What the scenario itself shows is this.
The self-healing test repairs its locators, which are the references used to find elements on the screen, and it still passes, even though the workflow now submits to the wrong endpoint.
In other words, the test went green while a real functional fault was present.
That is the situation option C describes: automatic repairs may mask critical functional defects in software.
Option D is the opposite of what happened here, since repairing a locator says nothing about whether the underlying logic is correct.
I am presenting that as the reading the scenario points to, not as a reviewed answer from the source.
Connecting this back to question fourteen, the same lesson applies.

Self-healing needs evidence in the form of change logs and coverage impact assessments, precisely because a passing result after an automatic repair does not by itself prove that business-critical behaviour is still correct.
